concepts.definition: SPI works with four lines: the clock (SCK), data from the Arduino (MOSI), data from the device (MISO) and CS, which selects the device.
concepts.example: On the Uno, SCK is D13, MISO D12, MOSI D11; in this lesson we connect the SD card's CS line to D10.
concepts.pitfall: Connecting LEDs to the SPI pins D11-D13 and using an SD card at the same time.

concepts.definition: Starts SPI and tries to talk to the card; returns true if it succeeds, false if not.
concepts.example: if (!SD.begin(10)) { Serial.println("kart yok"); } gives a warning if no card is found.
concepts.pitfall: Writing a CS pin different from the module's real connection; begin returns false.

concepts.definition: Opens the file for writing; if the file does not exist, it creates it; if it does, it adds the text to the end.
concepts.example: If you run the program twice, the second run's lines are added below the first run's.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking FILE_WRITE writes the file from the start and deletes the old data.

concepts.definition: A name of at most 8 characters, a dot and an extension of at most 3 characters; Turkish characters and spaces are not used.
concepts.example: VERI.CSV and LOG0001.TXT are valid names.
concepts.pitfall: Using a long name such as sicaklik_kaydi.csv; the file does not open, and if (dosya) catches this.

concepts.definition: Two commands that physically write the data waiting in the buffer to the card; close also closes the file.
concepts.example: In the open-write-close method, close() is called after every write, so the data is safe even if the power is cut.
concepts.pitfall: Removing the card or cutting the power without calling close() or flush(); the last lines are lost.

concepts.definition: SD cards work on 3.3 V; ready-made modules have a voltage regulator and a level shifter.
concepts.example: If the module's documentation says it can be used with a 5 V Arduino, the level shifter is built in.
concepts.pitfall: Connecting a bare SD card slot directly to the Arduino's 5 V pins.

quiz.prompt: On the Arduino Uno, which pins are the SCK, MISO and MOSI lines for SPI on?
options: SCK D11, MISO D12, MOSI D13
SCK D13, MISO D12, MOSI D11
SCK D10, MISO D11, MOSI D12
SCK A5, MISO A4, MOSI A3
quiz.explanation: On the Uno, SCK is D13, MISO D12 and MOSI D11; these pins are fixed. D10 was chosen for CS in this lesson; it is not an SPI line. A4 and A5 are the I2C lines (SDA, SCL).

quiz.prompt: Every time a program runs, it opens the file TEST.TXT with FILE_WRITE, writes two lines (println) and closes it. At the start the file does not exist. If the program is run three times, how many lines are in the file?
quiz.explanation: FILE_WRITE adds to the end of the file and does not delete the old contents. Each run adds 2 lines; 3 × 2 = 6 lines. If you assumed the file is written from the start, you would get 2; this is wrong.

options: The file name does not follow the 8.3 rule
FILE_READ should be used instead of FILE_WRITE
There is no close() or flush(); the data stays in the buffer and is not written to the card
print should be used instead of println
quiz.explanation: VERI.CSV follows the 8.3 rule (4 letters, a dot, 3 letters). The data first waits in the buffer in RAM; without close() or flush() it may not be written to the card. The only difference between print and println is the end of line; that is not the cause of the loss.

quiz.prompt: You want to connect the VCC and data pins of a bare SD card slot directly to the Uno's 5 V. What should you do?
options: No problem, SD cards work on 5 V
Connect the CS pin to 5 V
Do not do this; the card works with 3.3 V logic. Use a ready-made module with a voltage regulator and a level shifter
quiz.explanation: SD cards work with 3.3 V logic. Ready-made modules have a voltage regulator and a level shifter; a bare slot is never connected directly to the Arduino's 5 V. Check in its documentation that the module is suitable for 5 V.

quiz.prompt: Why is the "open-write-close" method counted as the safest against power cuts, compared with the "keep open and flush" method?
options: Because the file is closed after every write, so no data is left waiting in the buffer
Because the file uses no RAM at all
quiz.explanation: In the open-write-close method, close() is called after every line; no unwritten data is left in the buffer. In the keep open and flush method the data is also sent with flush; the difference is that the file stays open. It has nothing to do with speed or the file name rule.
